title: How the Web Works
summary: Follow one web address from your browser through DNS, the network, a server, and back into a rendered page.
learningOutcomes: Explain what a browser does after you enter a URL.
Separate DNS, transport security, HTTP, and rendering.
Locate a failure by the stage where it occurs.

heroVisual.title: A web page is a round trip
heroVisual.caption: The browser asks several systems for help before it can draw the result.

nodes.label: Address
nodes.detail: The URL identifies the scheme, host, path, and optional query.

nodes.label: Lookup
nodes.detail: DNS maps the host name to an address the network can route to.

nodes.label: Connection
nodes.detail: The browser creates a transport connection and usually protects it with TLS.

nodes.label: Request
nodes.detail: HTTP describes what resource the browser wants and what it can accept.

nodes.label: Response
nodes.detail: The server returns status, headers, and a body.

nodes.label: Render
nodes.detail: The browser parses resources, builds internal models, lays out, and paints.

sections.title: 1. The URL tells the browser where to begin
sections.summary: A URL is a structured address, not one undivided string.

blocks.text: When you press Enter, the browser first parses the address. It checks the scheme, normalizes the host, identifies the requested path, and decides whether a cached result, service worker, extension, or browser policy can answer before the network is used.

rows: Selects the protocol and security expectations.
Names a resource at that destination.
Points to a location inside the response; it is not sent in an HTTP request.
blocks.caption: The practical parts of a URL

blocks.title: URL versus domain
blocks.body: A domain is one part of a URL. The full URL can also contain a scheme, port, path, query, and fragment.

sections.title: 2. DNS finds a routable address
sections.summary: People use names; networks route to addresses.

items.title: Check nearby answers
items.explanation: The browser, operating system, and local network may already know the result.
items.result: A cached address can avoid a new lookup.

items.title: Ask a resolver
items.explanation: A recursive resolver follows or uses cached referrals through the DNS hierarchy.
items.result: It returns records such as A or AAAA.

items.title: Respect the lifetime
items.explanation: The record time-to-live controls how long an answer may be reused.
items.result: Later requests can use the cache until it expires.

blocks.title: DNS does not fetch the page
blocks.body: DNS answers where a named host can be reached. HTTP later asks that host for a resource.

items: A DNS error happens before an HTTP status exists.
Changing DNS can take time because valid cached answers remain until their lifetime ends.
One host name can map to multiple addresses for resilience or traffic distribution.

sections.title: 3. The browser creates a protected connection
sections.summary: Transport moves bytes; TLS protects their confidentiality and authenticity.

visual.title: Connection setup
visual.caption: Modern HTTP can use different transports, but the responsibilities remain distinct.

nodes.label: Route
nodes.detail: Packets travel across networks toward the destination.

nodes.label: Negotiate
nodes.detail: Client and server agree on transport and security details.

nodes.label: Authenticate
nodes.detail: The certificate helps the browser verify the server identity.

nodes.label: Protect
nodes.detail: Session keys encrypt later application data.

blocks.text: With HTTPS, the browser validates the server certificate and negotiates encryption before sensitive HTTP content is exchanged. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 commonly run over TCP plus TLS; HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which integrates transport and security differently.

blocks.caption: Do not collapse these layers into “the internet”

blocks.title: Debug from the outside inward
blocks.body: Confirm the URL, then DNS, then connection/TLS, then HTTP, then browser rendering. Each stage depends on the previous stage succeeding.

sections.title: 4. HTTP carries a meaningful request and response
sections.summary: HTTP messages explain intent and outcome.

blocks.code:
GET /guides/web HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Accept: text/html
blocks.explanation: A request method expresses the action, the target identifies the resource, and headers carry additional context.

blocks.code:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Cache-Control: max-age=300

<!doctype html>...
blocks.explanation: A response status summarizes the outcome, headers describe handling, and the body contains the representation.

items.title: Methods
items.summary: GET reads, POST submits, PUT replaces, PATCH changes part, and DELETE requests removal.
items.whenToUse: Choose the method whose semantics match the operation.

items.title: Status classes
items.summary: 1xx information, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client-side issue, 5xx server-side issue.
items.whenToUse: Use the class to locate responsibility before reading the exact code.
items.example: 404 means the selected resource was not found.

items.title: Headers
items.summary: Metadata controls representation, caching, authentication, content negotiation, and more.
items.whenToUse: Use standardized fields before inventing a custom protocol.

blocks.title: A successful connection can return an unsuccessful HTTP result
blocks.body: Receiving 404 or 500 proves that DNS, routing, connection, TLS, and enough HTTP communication worked to deliver the status.

sections.title: 5. The browser turns resources into pixels
sections.summary: A response is input; rendering is a separate pipeline.

items.title: Parse HTML
items.explanation: The browser builds a document tree from markup.

items.title: Resolve styles
items.explanation: CSS rules are matched and computed.
items.result: Each visible element receives final style values.

items.title: Run JavaScript
items.explanation: Scripts may read or change the document, styles, and application state.
items.result: The document can evolve after the first response.

items.title: Layout
items.explanation: The browser determines sizes and positions.

items.title: Paint and composite
items.explanation: Visual layers are drawn and combined.
items.result: Pixels appear and update on screen.

blocks.title: Loading is not one finish line
blocks.body: The first byte, first content, interactive state, and complete loading are different milestones. A fast server can still lead to a slow page if the browser has excessive work.

items: Reserve media space to prevent layout shifts.
Reduce blocking work needed for the first useful view.
Cache immutable assets with content-based file names.
Measure with real user conditions, not only a fast development computer.

sections.title: 6. Diagnose failures by stage
sections.summary: Symptoms become useful when mapped to the system that could produce them.

items: Reproduce with the exact URL and environment.
Inspect browser Network and Console evidence.
Change one cause at a time.
Verify the original symptom after the fix.

glossary.definition: A client application that requests, interprets, and presents web resources.
The distributed naming system that maps domain names to records such as IP addresses.
An application protocol that defines request and response semantics.
A protocol that authenticates peers and protects data in transit.
The browser work that converts document, style, script, and media inputs into a visual result.
